entries.name: unbound-check-removed
entries.claim: The rule's unbound half is what refuses a declared permission nothing acknowledges: skipping the branch body with a bare continue leaves a permission declared on the composed application, or on the v0 shell, with no acknowledgement compiling silently -- the exact vacuum R7 named, with nothing thrown and nothing emitted. The unretainable-package control dies with it for the same reason: an empty acknowledgement is only strict because this branch fires, so defeating it makes 'empty refuses everything' false.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: a permission the composed application declares and nothing acknowledges refuses the release by name
kills.expected: a declared permission that nothing binds and nothing acknowledges must refuse compilation

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: the rule runs at language v0 too — the shell demo builds under its acknowledgement and refuses an unacknowledged permission by name
kills.expected: a v0 package declaring an unacknowledged permission must refuse compilation

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: removing the acknowledgement of a permission the package still declares refuses it by name
kills.expected: a declared permission whose acknowledgement was removed must be refused by name

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: a recorded revision from an unlisted package is judged unretainable, not crashed on
kills.expected: an empty acknowledgement refuses every declared permission by name

entries.name: governance-wiring-removed
entries.claim: The whole-model wiring in compiler.ts is the only path by which an acknowledgement reaches the rule: making the condition unreachable leaves every governed compile ungoverned, so an unacknowledged permission compiles on the composed application and on the v0 shell, a mislabelled acknowledgement no longer refuses, and a release compile handed nullish is admitted. It varies ONE property -- whether the wiring fires -- and deliberately leaves the fixture path's behaviour (no acknowledgement, no governance) unchanged, so the census control survives and the kill set is exactly the governed claims.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: a permission the composed application declares and nothing acknowledges refuses the release by name
kills.expected: a declared permission that nothing binds and nothing acknowledges must refuse compilation

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: the rule runs at language v0 too — the shell demo builds under its acknowledgement and refuses an unacknowledged permission by name
kills.expected: a v0 package declaring an unacknowledged permission must refuse compilation

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: an acknowledgement for another package, or an unreadable one, fails closed rather than ungoverning
kills.expected: a mislabelled acknowledgement must refuse the compile rather than ungovern it

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: the release entry point governs unconditionally, so casting around its required parameter is refused rather than ungoverned
kills.expected: must be refused, never ungoverned

entries.name: subject-check-removed
entries.claim: The explicit subject is what makes a mislabelled acknowledgement fail closed: comparing the acknowledgement's packageId against itself instead of the compiled package's id accepts an acknowledgement written for any package, which is the missing-key-means-ungoverned defect round 1 was blocked on, one level up.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: an acknowledgement for another package, or an unreadable one, fails closed rather than ungoverning
kills.expected: an acknowledgement naming another package must refuse this one by name

entries.name: stale-check-removed
entries.claim: The rule's stale half is what refuses an entry naming a permission the package does not declare: testing membership in the acknowledgement itself instead of in the declared census makes the branch unreachable, and a stale entry then survives compilation.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: an entry naming a permission the package does not declare is stale, whether or not its resource exists
kills.expected: an acknowledgement naming a permission the package does not declare must be refused as stale

entries.name: evaluator-binding-removed
entries.claim: Removing the exact party_create evaluator binding while the composed application still declares it refuses the release by that permission's name. The empty acknowledgement cannot conceal a missing implementation binding.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: the unchanged composed application builds only with its exact evaluator-binding census
kills.expected: COMPILER_PERMISSION_EVALUATOR_UNBOUND.*northstar\.app:permission\.party_create

entries.name: stale-active-binding-added
entries.claim: An active evaluator binding naming a permission the package does not declare refuses the unchanged release as stale. Only exact compatible-extension bindings may precede their dependent declaration.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: the unchanged composed application builds only with its exact evaluator-binding census
kills.expected: COMPILER_PERMISSION_ACKNOWLEDGEMENT_STALE.*northstar\.app:permission\.stock_count_probe_stale

entries.name: governed-package-key-renamed
entries.claim: A one-character typo in the checked-in list's package key must stop the release build itself, not only a later test: the loader refuses before compiling, so the real release script's --check on an untouched copy of the inputs goes red, and every test that reads the composed package's entries through the loader dies with it. Every control that reads the composed package's entries through the loader dies with it, including the release entry point's admission assertion and the narrowing control.

kills.name: unbound-permission release script: check:app-release on an untouched copy of the release inputs is green
kills.expected: names no entries for package northstar\.app:package\.application;

entries.name: release-governance-made-optional
entries.claim: The RELEASE entry point's `required` governance is what closes round 2's fail-open defect: downgrading compileApplicationRelease to the caller-supplied contract makes a release compile handed a nullish acknowledgement compile green instead of refusing, which is exactly the absent-admission-input bypass the round-2 review blocked on.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: the release entry point governs unconditionally, so casting around its required parameter is refused rather than ungoverned
kills.expected: must be refused, never ungoverned

entries.name: recorded-revision-narrowing-removed
entries.claim: Narrowing the checked-in evaluator bindings to a recorded revision's own census is what lets --truncate-invalid-lineage govern historical entries at all: returning current active bindings unnarrowed reports every newer binding as stale against an older revision.

kills.name: unbound-permission acknowledgement: a recorded revision is governed by the checked-in list narrowed to its own census, which can only shrink it
kills.expected: narrowing keeps exactly the evaluator bindings the revision declares

kills.name: --truncate-invalid-lineage governs recorded revisions: it narrows to each revision census and drops one declaring an unacknowledged permission
kills.expected: truncation failed

entries.name: truncation-acknowledgement-self-certified
entries.claim: Truncation must govern a recorded revision against the CHECKED-IN list narrowed to that revision, never against evidence derived from the revision itself. Deriving it from the revision's own census satisfies the required parameter tautologically and admits a recorded release declaring a permission nothing ever acknowledged -- the self-certifying shape round 3's review named as a live limit. The observable consequence is exact and is what this entry declares: the revision that governance should have refused instead COMPILES, and is then caught one step later by the serialization comparison as `applications[1] does not match its current compiler output`. The red therefore proves governance was defeated on this route, not merely that something went wrong.

kills.name: --truncate-invalid-lineage governs recorded revisions: it narrows to each revision census and drops one declaring an unacknowledged permission
kills.expected: applications\[1\] does not match its current compiler output
